deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. On the previous page (54r) Riemann works with integrals of the type F(s)=∫_0^∞ e^{-x²i} x^{s} dx/(e^{x√π}-e^{-x√π}), i.e. Mordell-type integrals. He expresses ξ(s) through them; the page writes μ(−s) as a multiple of such an integral. On this page he takes the s-value α−ti together with its 'conjugate' partner at α+ti. This is the route to |F|² on a vertical line, which a mean-value or zero study of ξ would need.

(1) PRODUCT AS A DOUBLE INTEGRAL. Riemann sets
P = ∫_0^∞ e^{-ix²} x^{α-ti} dx/(2 sinh(x√π)) · ∫_0^∞ e^{+iy²} y^{α+ti} dy/(2 sinh(y√π)).
He substitutes x=r(1+z), y=r(1−z), with r∈(0,∞) and z∈(−1,1); this covers the quadrant x,y>0 exactly once. He computes the partial derivatives x_r=1+z, x_z=r, y_r=1−z, y_z=−r, so the Jacobian is x_r y_z − y_r x_z = −2r and |J|=2r. The pieces transform as follows:
- x^{α−ti} y^{α+ti} = r^{2α}(1+z)^{α−ti}(1−z)^{α+ti};
- with the Jacobian this gives the factor 2r^{1+2α};
- the exponent is −ix²+iy² = −ir²[(1+z)²−(1−z)²] = −4zr²i.
Hence
P = 2∫_0^∞∫_{−1}^{1} e^{−4zr²i} r^{1+2α}(1+z)^{α−ti}(1−z)^{α+ti} dz dr / [(e^{(1+z)r√π}−e^{−(1+z)r√π})(e^{(1−z)r√π}−e^{−(1−z)r√π})].
The page writes e^{−2zr r i}; this is a slip, corrected to e^{−4zrri} on the next page.

(2) INNER r-INTEGRAL BY RESIDUES. This is what the sketches show: the axis picture and the sector contour with an arrow toward −∞.
- For fixed z>0, e^{−4zr²i} decays in the sector −π/2<arg r<0. So the r-ray can be rotated onto the imaginary axis.
- The ray passes poles of the first factor at (1+z)r√π = nπi, i.e. r = n i√π/(1+z), r² = −n²π/(1+z)².
- The derivative of the first denominator there is 2(1+z)√π cosh(nπi) = 2(−1)^n(1+z)√π.
- The second factor becomes e^{(1−z)r√π} = e^{s nπi}, with s := (1−z)/(1+z).
- In the exponent, (my step) 4z/(1+z)² = 1−s². So 2z n²π i/(1+z)² = ½n²πi − ½s²n²πi. These are exactly the terms Riemann obtains using his factor −2z.
The residue sum picked up is therefore
(−2πi) Σ_n e^{−½s²n²πi + ½n²πi} / [(1+z)√π · 2(−1)^n · (e^{snπi} − e^{−snπi})].
Riemann suppresses the factors r^{1+2α}(1+z)^{α−ti}(1−z)^{α+ti}; at the pole these would contribute powers of n and z. He keeps only the exponential/denominator 'kernel'.
The map s=(1−z)/(1+z) takes z=1→0, z=0→1 and z=−1→∞; it is a Möbius map, whence the circle/line sketch with the labels z=∞, −1, 1, 0.

(3) THE KERNEL AS A FUNCTION OF s.
- The first attempt, f(s) = Σ e^{−½s²n²πi+½n²πi+nπi}/(e^{snπi}−e^{−snπi}), and its v-shifted variant are crossed out.
- He then studies the cosine-denominator analogue
f(s,v) = Σ_{n∈Z} e^{−½(sn+v)²πi} / (e^{(sn+v)πi}+e^{−(sn+v)πi}),
together with the theta function φ(s,v) = Σ_n e^{−½(sn+v)²πi}.
- f(s,v)=f(s,s+v) follows from the shift n→n+1.
- For f(s,v+2), put w=sn+v. Then e^{−½(w+2)²πi} = e^{−½w²πi−2wπi}. Using e^{−2wπi} = e^{−wπi}(e^{wπi}+e^{−wπi}) − 1, each term equals e^{−½w²πi−wπi} − (original term).
- Completing the square, −½w²πi−wπi = −½(w+1)²πi + ½πi.
- Hence f(s,v+2) = e^{πi/2} φ(s,v+1) − f(s,v).
- Iterating with f(s,v) = iφ(s,v−1) − f(s,v−2) gives f(s,v+2) = iφ(s,v+1) − iφ(s,v−1) + f(s,v−2). The sign in front of the second φ is overwritten on the page and must be minus.
This is a quasi-periodicity (elliptic transformation) law for a Lerch-type sum, with a theta function as the correction term. Presumably Riemann intended to combine it with s→1/s or s→s+2 transformations to sum the residue series in closed form.
errors: The exponent after substitution is written e^{−2zr²i}; correctly −ix²+iy² = −4zr²i. Riemann fixes this on the next page. Consequently the residue exponent should be n²πi(1−s²), not ½n²πi(1−s²), unless rescaled.

In the residue computation the factors r^{1+2α}(1+z)^{α−ti}(1−z)^{α+ti} are silently dropped (they give n-dependent powers at r=n i√π/(1+z)). This is an intentional simplification to study the kernel, but it is not justified as an identity.

Residues from the poles of the second factor ((1−z)r√π = mπi) are not visibly treated. Neither is convergence of the rotated contour where the quadratic exponential does not decay (z<0 needs the opposite rotation).
The series f(s,v) and φ(s,v) converge only for suitable complex s (|e^{−½s²n²πi}| decays only if Im(s²)<0). Denominators vanish when (sn+v) is half an odd integer. None of this is addressed.
In the final iterated relation the sign before e^{πi/2}φ(s,v−1) must be minus; the page shows an overwritten sign.

results.what: Product of two Mordell-type integrals (the s and 'conjugate' values on Re=α) turned into a double integral via x=r(1+z), y=r(1−z), with Jacobian −2r
results.modern_name: Polar-type change of variables for a mean square |F(α+it)|²; Mordell integral
results.usually_credited_to: Mordell integrals: Mordell 1920s/1933 (Kronecker, Riemann earlier). Riemann's use of such integrals for ζ was published by Siegel in 1932.

results.what: Evaluation of the inner r-integral by contour rotation and residues at r=n i√π/(1+z), giving a theta-quotient series in s=(1−z)/(1+z)
results.modern_name: Residue evaluation leading to an Appell–Lerch-type sum
results.usually_credited_to: Standard technique (Cauchy). The Riemann–Siegel integral manipulations are credited to Riemann via Siegel 1932.

results.what: f(s,v)=Σ e^{−½(sn+v)²πi}/(2cos π(sn+v)) satisfies f(s,v)=f(s,s+v) and f(s,v+2)=iφ(s,v+1)−f(s,v), with φ a theta function
results.modern_name: Quasi-periodicity (elliptic transformation) of an Appell–Lerch sum with theta correction; cf. Zwegers' μ-function
results.usually_credited_to: Appell (1884–86) and Lerch (1892) for these sums; the systematic theory is due to Zwegers (2002)

deep.surprise_reason: Riemann's use of Mordell-type integrals in the ξ/Riemann–Siegel context is known through Siegel. However, attacking the mean square |F(α+it)|² this way, and arriving at an Appell–Lerch-type sum with its theta-corrected quasi-periodicity, predates Appell and Lerch. That is a notable unpublished detail, though the individual computations are elementary and the attempt is fragmentary.

checkable.asserts: −ix²+iy² = −4zr²i, i.e. Riemann's −2zr²i on this page is a slip (result 0).
Derivative of the first denominator at the pole r=n i√π/(1+z) equals 2(−1)^n(1+z)√π (result 0).
Termwise identity behind f(s,v+2) = iφ(s,v+1) − f(s,v) (result 0).
Beta integral used on the next page for the z-integral (result 0).

transcription_corrections: The exponent e^{−2zrri} in the double integral is correctly read; it is Riemann's own slip, corrected to −4zrri on the next page.
Final line: the operator before e^{πi/2}φ(s,v−1) is an overwritten sign; mathematically it must be '−', giving f(s,v+2)=e^{πi/2}φ(s,v+1)−e^{πi/2}φ(s,v−1)+f(s,v−2).

In the residue line, 'rr = −nnπ/(1+z)²' and '(1+z)r√π = nπi' are correct. The denominator should read (1+z)√π·2(−1)^n·(e^{snπi}−e^{−snπi}); the order of the two exponentials is ambiguous in the image.
The fragment '−2zrri = +2z nnπ i/(1+z)² = ... ½nnπi − ½((1−z)/(1+z))² nnπi' contains a struck-out intermediate (nnπi − (1−z)/(1+z) nnπi); the surviving equality is ½nnπi − ½s²nnπi.
